overview:
It began with a street vendor. On 17 December 2010 Mohamed Bouazizi, humiliated by municipal officials in the Tunisian town of Sidi Bouzid, set himself on fire; within a month of protests President Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali, in power for twenty-three years, had fled to Saudi Arabia. The grievances that carried the news outward were not peculiar to Tunisia — young populations with more education than employment, food price inflation, entrenched security states, and ruling families whose corruption was an open secret. Satellite television, above all Al Jazeera, and social networks let Tunisians watch each other and then let Egyptians, Yemenis, Libyans, Bahrainis and Syrians watch Tunisia. By February 2011 Cairo's Tahrir Square had forced out Hosni Mubarak after thirty years; by autumn Muammar Gaddafi was dead, hunted down after an eight-month civil war fought with NATO air support; Yemen's Ali Abdullah Saleh signed away his office under a Gulf-brokered deal that took formal effect in February 2012.

Where rulers had money, loyal armies or powerful patrons, the outcome was different. In Bahrain, protesters occupying the Pearl Roundabout from 14 February 2011 were cleared after Saudi and Emirati troops crossed the causeway on 14 March under the Gulf Cooperation Council's Peninsula Shield Force; a royally commissioned inquiry later documented 46 deaths, hundreds of torture allegations and thousands of dismissals and detentions. In Syria, protests that started in Deraa in March 2011 met live fire and hardened, by mid-2012, into a civil war that drew in Iran, Russia, Turkey, the Gulf states and the United States, killed hundreds of thousands and displaced more than eleven million. Elsewhere the tremors were smaller but real: monarchs in Morocco and Jordan conceded constitutional revisions, Algeria lifted its long state of emergency, and Iran's opposition tried unsuccessfully in February 2011 to revive the crushed Green Movement of 2009. Some scholars push the starting point earlier still, to the Gdeim Izik protest camp of October–November 2010, where some fifteen thousand Sahrawis camped outside El Aaiún in Western Sahara before Moroccan forces dismantled it — a claim that remains a minority reading rather than a settled one.

The reversal came quickly. Egypt's elected Islamist president Mohamed Morsi faced mass protests through 2012 and into 2013 and was removed by the army, opening a harsher authoritarianism than the one overthrown; Libya, Syria and Yemen fragmented into wars that outlasted the decade. Commentators reached for the phrase "Arab Winter." Tunisia, where it started, was the one state to build a functioning democracy from the uprising — and even there the achievement proved fragile, eroded by economic stagnation and, after 2021, by a president governing largely by decree.
significance: For a few months in 2011 the assumption that Arab authoritarianism was permanent simply collapsed, and four long-serving rulers fell in a year — something no Cold War-era analysis of the region had predicted. The consequences reached far beyond the Arab world: the Syrian war produced the largest refugee movement since 1945 and reshaped European politics; Libya's collapse fed arms and fighters into the Sahel; the Islamic State grew in the wreckage of Syria and Iraq; and the Gulf states, especially Saudi Arabia and the UAE, drew the lesson that counter-revolution was worth funding abroad, a policy that shaped the next decade of Middle Eastern politics. It also became the reference case in arguments about whether social media makes revolutions, why mass mobilisation topples rulers but rarely builds institutions, and how quickly a security state can reconstitute itself.
coverage: Written from general reference works (Britannica, Wikipedia) and retrospective institutional assessments, chiefly the Council on Foreign Relations' ten-year review, plus the Bahrain Independent Commission of Inquiry for Bahrain's casualty and detention figures. The dataset's eight events are a skewed sample: they omit Tunisia, where the uprising began, and Yemen, while including the 2011–12 Iranian protests and an alleged Abu Dhabi palace coup attested mainly by a single later interview. More broadly, casualty figures for Syria and Libya are estimates with wide ranges, much of the documentary record for Syria and Bahrain comes through state or opposition channels rather than neutral observers, and scholars still disagree about causes — economic grievance, demography, media, or contingency — and about when the events should be said to have started or ended.
